passage: Last term I, Rekha, couldn't look at Charu without my ears burning. When Charu walked past our desk I stared at my geometry box and pretended it was fascinating. My friends noticed and teased me, which made it worse. Charu sent me a friendly "hey, did you do the map homework?" and I read it about fifteen times, trying to find a hidden meaning that was probably not there. Did the smiley mean anything? Was I imagining it? Finally I asked, plainly and quietly, "I like you a lot. Is that okay with you?" Charu said, "I really like you as a friend." It stung, but I said, "Thanks for telling me," and we stayed friends. I told my cousin, and she just hugged me.

qa.q: What did Rekha pretend to be fascinated by when Charu walked past?
qa.a: Rekha pretended the geometry box was fascinating.

qa.q: Why did Rekha read Charu's text so many times?
qa.a: Rekha hoped there was a hidden meaning, feeling attracted and unable to tell what the friendly message meant. Rekha may also have been nervous and needed reassurance.

qa.q: What did Rekha do that showed respect?
qa.a: Rekha asked plainly and quietly whether Charu was okay with those feelings, and accepted Charu's answer without arguing or pressing.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt when Rekha asked?
qa.a: Charu may have felt surprised or a bit uneasy, and also grateful that Rekha asked kindly and accepted no.

grounding: A teen's first attraction shows in blushing, avoidance and unclear texts, and respect means asking and accepting no.

passage: Counsellor's note, Wednesday. Payal came in twisting her ring. She told me she had liked a boy in the next section, and they started texting. At first it was fun; his messages were teasing and she blushed. Then he began asking for photos she was not comfortable sending. When she said no, he replied, "If you like me you would." She is unsure whether he means harm or is just being awkward, and she felt embarrassed about having liked him. I told her that a no should be accepted, that liking someone does not mean owing them anything, and that she did the right thing coming to me. With her permission, I have called her parents in to talk together. Indu.

qa.q: What was Payal twisting when she came in?
qa.a: She was twisting her ring.

qa.q: What might Payal be worried about after his reply?
qa.a: She may worry that she has done something wrong and that he might be angry, and she is embarrassed about her first crush. She is also unsure what he means.

qa.q: What should Payal do if the messages continue?
qa.a: Keep saying no, save the messages and let a trusted adult such as her counsellor or parents handle it.

qa.q: How might the boy see his own texts?
qa.a: He may think he is just showing interest, but pressing after a no is not acceptable, whatever his intention.

grounding: A first crush turns into unclear pressure and an unsafe request, and a trusted adult supports her.

passage:
Wednesday
Okay, diary, facts first. Pranav sat next to me in library period three times this week. He keeps teasing my handwriting ("doctor scribble"). Today he sent me a meme at 11 pm about exams, just to me.
Also facts: my face goes hot when he laughs. I've started taking the long way to class so I pass the lab where he sits.
Does it mean anything? He might just be friendly. He teases everyone. Sending memes might mean nothing at all.
So I did the scary thing. After school I asked, "Hey, do you like me in a more-than-friends way? Totally fine if not."
He went a bit red and said, "I really like you as a friend. Just friend. Is that okay?"
I said yes. It stings a bit. But he wasn't mean, and I asked instead of guessing for another month.
- Nilesh

qa.q: How many times did Pranav sit next to Nilesh in library period this week?
qa.a: Pranav sat next to Nilesh three times this week.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling after Pranav's answer?
qa.a: Nilesh felt a sting of disappointment but also some relief and pride at having asked instead of guessing.

qa.q: Which choice of Nilesh's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking directly and saying "Totally fine if not" worked, because the signals were unclear and it gave Pranav an easy, pressure-free way to answer honestly.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt being asked?
qa.a: Pranav probably felt surprised and a little awkward, going red, but also respected because Nilesh made it safe to say no.

grounding: The diary shows first attraction with unclear signals, and the teenager asking directly and accepting a no.

passage:
Every morning at the Dhamtari bus stand, Tanvir stood as far from Trisha as he could, then somehow ended up right beside her by the time the bus came.
He teased her about her cycle bell ("sounds like a sick goat"), went red when she laughed, and then spent the whole ride staring out of the window.
Trisha couldn't work it out. Was he annoyed with her? Was it a joke? Her friend Ruchi said, "He likes you, obviously." Trisha wasn't sure anything was obvious.
On Friday she asked him straight. "Tanvir, are you teasing me because I annoy you, or something else?"
He looked at his shoes. "Something else."
Trisha took a breath. "I don't feel that way. But I like talking to you."
Tanvir nodded, cheeks burning. "Okay. Fair. Can I still say the bell's a goat?"
"You can."

qa.q: What did Tanvir say Trisha's cycle bell sounded like?
qa.a: He said it sounded like a sick goat.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling about Tanvir's behaviour before Friday?
qa.a: She felt confused and unsure, because his teasing, blushing and avoidance could mean he was annoyed or that he liked her.

qa.q: Which choice worked well for both of them?
qa.a: Trisha asking directly cleared up the unclear signals, and Tanvir accepting her no with a joke kept the friendship easy.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have been feeling when he admitted it was "something else"?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed and nervous, looking at his shoes with burning cheeks, but he respected her answer.

grounding: The scene shows a crush shown through teasing, blushing and avoidance, and a direct question with a no that is accepted.

passage: In the corridors of their Nairobi secondary school, Chen had a new habit: whenever Wanjiru walked by, he suddenly needed to tie a shoelace that was already tied. In chemistry he teased her about her spiky handwriting, then went red to the ears when she laughed. At night he typed long messages and sent only "did u get the homework". Otieno said, "She likes you, obviously. She sat next to you on the bus." Chen wasn't sure. She sat next to everyone. On Friday, by the bike rack, he made himself ask. "I kind of like you. Like, like-like. Do you feel the same, or no?" Wanjiru looked surprised, then kind. "I like you as a friend, Chen. Not that way. Sorry." His face burned. "Okay. Thanks for telling me straight." On Monday he said hi to her normally, and meant it.

qa.q: What did Chen send at night after typing long messages?
qa.a: Chen sent only "did u get the homework".

qa.q: What was Chen feeling each time Wanjiru walked by?
qa.a: Chen was most likely nervous and shy because of a crush, shown by the fake shoelace tying and going red; it could also be plain awkwardness, which is why asking mattered.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Chen asked directly instead of trusting Otieno's guess, and accepted Wanjiru's no politely, so their friendship could carry on.

qa.q: What might Wanjiru have needed when Chen asked?
qa.a: Wanjiru needed room to answer honestly without pressure, and Chen thanking her and greeting her normally on Monday gave her that.

grounding: It shows a first crush coming out as blushing, teasing and avoidance, unclear signals from the other side, and respect meaning asking directly and accepting a no.
